newsitem.title: USA: U.S. praises Hong Kong govenor-elect.
newsitem.headline: U.S. praises Hong Kong govenor-elect.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday congratulated Tung Chee-hwa, a shipping tycoon newly elected to be Hong Kong's governor, calling him a man of "integrity and independent thinking."

Noting that Tung was the first Hong Kong governor to be elected rather than appointed by Britain, State Department spokesman Glyn Davies made no reference to pro-democracy protests against the Beijing-orchestrated vote.

"We look forward to working closely with Mr. Tung to further U.S. interests in Hong Kong, and to contribute to Hong Kong's further stability, prosperity and democratic development," Davies told reporters.

"He enjoys the respect of Americans for his integrity and independent thinking and we expect he will take seriously his role to preserve Hong Kong's rule of law and high degree of autonomy after reversion," Davies said.
Under a joint declaration between Britain and China, the colony reverts to Chinese rule in July of next year.
Tung's election by members of a 400-strong electoral college assembled by the Beijing government was widely regarded in Hong Kong as a foregone conclusion.
Tung, whose family maritime empire was bailed out by Beijing a decade ago, had been regarded as China's man since he was singled out for a handshake by China's President Jiang Zemin in January.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said that while the selection process that chose Tung was "certainly not democratic," it followed "the measures that have been jointly negotiated between the British and the Chinese."

Outside the hall where the election took place, noisy pro-democracy activists denounced the process as a travesty and set fire to a replica of a traditional Chinese tomb symbolising what they said was the death of democracy.

"Our interests in Hong Kong, which are significant and which include substantial financial investments on the part of the United States ... reflect our desire to see continued promotion of democratic institutions ... We will continue to make that point as we have dialogue with the government of China on the future of Hong Kong," McCurry said.
